#1053. Bayern Munich's Kenya friendly highlights Africa's growing pull for global sport

Bayern Munich are to open Nairobi's new Raila Odinga International Stadium against Ajax as Kenya prepares for AFCON 2027. The match highlights Africa's growing sports ambitions — and questions over cost and legacy.

Bundesliga champions Bayern Munich are to travel to Nairobi, Kenya during the winter break to play a friendly that opens the newly finished Raila Odinga International Stadium in the capital city. The German side will face Ajax Amsterdam as the game acts as part of the country's preparations for the 2027 African Cup of Nations (AFCON), which will be held in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania next summer.

"Bayern has millions of fantastic fans in Africa with whom we feel a close connection – it's a continent with a huge passion for football," Rouven Kasper, Bayern board member for marketing and sales, said in a club statement.

"We will be making a further contribution to raising the profile of the Bundesliga and are very much looking forward to this special event."

The news is just the latest venture into global sports investing in Africa. Earlier this month, Formula 1 announced it was returning to the continent after Rwanda secured the rights for a deal from the early 2030s onwards. In September, World Athletics revealed Nairobi would host the World Championships in 2029. It will be the first time the event has been held in Africa.

Simon Chadwick, a business management and program director at the African School of Economics, believes that over the last two decades the professionalization and industrialization of sports has begun to emerge in Africa.

"Countries like Rwanda, Kenya, Morocco and obviously, South Africa, if we go back to the last decade of the previous century, have increasingly begun to deploy sport as a policy instrument," Chadwick told DW, adding Senegal and Egypt to the list.

"There are these image and reputational benefits which very often are bundled up as soft power. It's about attractiveness and appeal and engagement," said Chadwick.

"It's almost like a kind of professionalization, industrialization and politicization of sport that we're seeing elsewhere in the world has now arrived in Africa. We are seeing a much greater sense of kind of self-determination within Africa to do this," he added.

"This is not just about sport. It is also about diplomacy and bilateral trade, but also about the broader economic and industrial context within which sport sits."

For Kenya specifically, the building of the stadium is in line with the housing and sports infrastructural development that has been so heavily promoted under President William Ruto. Hosting this game is a symbol of the development currently happening in Nairobi.

"The bigger picture is that Nairobi now is positioning itself as a as an alternative sports venue," Richard Wanjohi, Editorial and Research Lead at the African Sports and Creative Institute (ASCI), told DW.

"I think we have seen what Kigali has done over the last number of years. For us to then come back into this conversation as a major city that can host such an event, it's huge. A few weeks later, we'll have the rugby sevens series again and then ultimately, the Africa Cup of Nations in July."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chadwick believes that unlike Rwanda, Kenya's relative stability and pre-existing tourist industry allows for a more natural development of sports investment.

"This is not Kenya trying to build a tourism industry through an engagement in sport. I think it's an extension of what Kenya has been doing for a number of years through sport."

Combined with being a multi-sport country - athletics, rugby, football, volleyball – Wanjohi believes Kenya is ready to make the most of that performance on the field or track.

"It's about time that we also host the world and show them that we can do this from a hosting perspective, but also from developing infrastructure that is ready to host such sports events," Wanjohi said.

"It's beyond just saying that we have the talent that is already in the sport, but it's saying that we have the infrastructure, we have the skills, we have the capability to host this as any other African, if not global nation."

However, Ruto's government has been criticized over taxation, unemployment and its handling of dissent. Given that this stadium cost approximately €375 million ($418 million), it is perhaps no surprise that questions are being asked about the decision to invest in major sports infrastructure.

"People are asking, we are a struggling economy. There are a lot of other issues that could be addressed, like the education sector, health and all that. How did we get that money and be able to make that provision? Also interestingly, is that there's an appearance fee that is going to be paid to both Bayern and Ajax," said Wanjohi, who added there was also some frustration that the opening game was not given to local teams or even the national side.

Ultimately, the timing of this also matters. While many sports fans in the country are excited, others are critical.

"The government knows that this is almost like a campaign tool. We have an election coming up in August next year so the government or the president of the day obviously wants to use as much leverage of such an event to milk it for all it's worth," Wanjohi added.

"So the two different schools of thought are: It's a good thing to have, but at what cost are we doing it at and is it in the public interest as well?"

The proof will be in what the legacy of events like Bayern Munich's friendly in Nairobi brings Kenyan football. The feeling in late 2026 though, is largely optimistic.

"I guess the acid test is that many African nations carry with them the baggage from the past that this is just trophy asset investment that is ultimately going to create white, white elephant infrastructure," Chadwick said.

"But having spoken to people in Kenyan sport, in the industry itself, it seems to me that there is a genuine appetite for sports to become a genuine and legitimate driver of economic activity."

Janek Speight contributed reporting for this article.

Former Chelsea captain John Terry has become an investor in MatchWornShirt

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Sports memorabilia platform MatchWornShirt has secured new backing from a group of active and former footballers, alongside North American sports investors.

Announced on Tuesday, the funding round is led by Gamma Waves Partners, a global sports and technology investment platform founded by former Italy defender Giorgio Chiellini, Andrea Agnelli and Rocco Benetton.

Former Chelsea and England captain John Terry and current Tottenham Hotspur defender Tosin Adarabioyo have invested individually. Premier League brothers Jurrien Timber (Arsenal), and Quinten Timber (Crystal Palace), have also joined the round through Joyned Capital, a private investment club for professional athletes.

Outside football, the investment group includes basketball player Kevin Durant and Rich Kleiman’s 35V, along with the ownership group behind the NBA's Indiana Pacers and WNBA's Indiana Fever.

The capital injection follows a year in which MWS expanded its physical presence in North America ahead of the 2026 World Cup and agreed inaugural partnerships in the NBA, WNBA, NFL and NHL.

MWS were founded in Amsterdam in 2017 by brothers Tijmen and Bob Zonderwijk, the idea initially coming about during a search for an Ajax shirt for their father.

The company now partners with more than 450 clubs worldwide to auction authentic, game-worn items.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“I first got involved in match-worn shirts by selling them for charity, seeing the unique emotional value these items hold for fans,” Chiellini said. “Today, it is exciting to see the category evolve, as collectors increasingly recognise the significance and value of these pieces of sporting history.

“MatchWornShirt is building the infrastructure to connect fans and collectors with authentic moments from sport, while helping sports organisations unlock new value from their intellectual property. We are excited to support the company's next phase of growth.”

MWS co-founder and CEO Tijmen Zonderwijk said the incoming shareholders align with the platform’s long-term strategy.

“The scale of the names and businesses involved in this group of investors demonstrates a collective passion for what we have already built here at MWS, and for that, we're incredibly proud,” he said.

“It also represents a shared vision for the future, and we're excited to accelerate the growth of the business whilst remaining true to our values.”

The individual size of Terry and co's investment has not been disclosed at this time.

#1051. Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row

The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes

They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year.

Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running, but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.

As the Top 100 approaches a decade since its inception, nobody has quite dominated an era like Bonmatí and, while 2025 did not end in major silverware on the European stage, there were moments of sublime brilliance on the way to a Champions League final as well as the Euro one with Spain.

Bonmatí, as the very best do, has become a figure who can step up when needed most, and has become synonymous with the Blaugrana Barcelona stripes, a one-club woman with over 300 appearances in all competitions for the Catalan giants. Catalonia born and bred, both her parents were teachers of the Catalan language, with Bonmatí’s life and career intertwined with the region since she was a child, and now she has become an icon not just at home, but all around the world.

In a time where the women’s game is growing exponentially and world class talents are queueing up to dethrone the midfielder, she remains at the top. However, having broken a leg in training before the Nations League final she will miss more than four months of 2026. She will be sorely missed.

It was a tighter margin of victory in 2025, 453 points ahead of compatriot Mariona Caldentey – compared to 568 last year ahead of Caroline Graham Hansen – with the Spanish duo plus Alessia Russo and Putellas all gaining over 4,000 points from our record panel of 143 judges.

Bonmatí received 43% of the No 1 votes, ahead of Caldentey with a 21% share. Russo and Putellas both had 8% of the first picks in third and fourth respectively.

In a year where England backed up their Euro 2022 success with victory in Switzerland, Brazil continued their dominance in South America and Nigeria regained supremacy in Africa, it was all change across the top 100 as players such as Caldentey, Russo, Hannah Hampton, Temwa Chawinga, Patri Guijarro, Ewa Pajor and Clàudia Pina all made a new-look top 10 for the first time.

The Barcelona starlet Pina was the biggest mover, up 65 places on 2024, followed by another Spaniard in Gotham FC striker Esther González, up 59, while Klara Bühl moved up 40, just ahead of Russo’s 39 to propel the Arsenal striker into the top three.

Ghizlane Chebbak gave Morocco a first ever entry into the top 100 and Canada’s new Northern Super League was represented in its first year thanks to the Nigerian striker Esther Okoronkwo of AFC Toronto.

In fact, almost a quarter of this year’s 100 were brand new faces, emphasising just how fast the women’s game is growing, with the Chelsea and England shot-stopper Hampton the highest of the new names, shooting straight into the top five after her Euro-winning performances, while Vicky López, Sofia Cantore, Nathalie Björn and Michelle Agyemang all made the top 50.

Performances on the continental stage earned first-time appearances for the likes of Okoronkwo, Brazil’s Amanda Gutierres and Nigeria’s Gift Monday, while potential stars of the future such as Olivia Smith, Lily Yohannes and Signe Gaupset ranked for the first time. Mexico’s Charlyn Corral gained long overdue recognition.

Others made their way back into the 100, such as the Arsenal and England duo Leah Williamson and Chloe Kelly after a trophy-laden 12 months while Sandy Baltimore and Cristiana Girelli also made returns straight into the top quarter.

Lucy Bronze, Wendie Renard and Pernille Harder remain the only three players to have maintained a place every year after Saki Kumagai and Jenni Hermoso dropped out for the first time and it was Bronze’s Chelsea who dethroned Barcelona as the team with the most representatives with 15 compared to Arsenal’s 14 and Barcelona’s 12 after a domestic treble for Sonia Bompastor’s side.

Unsurprisingly after another Euro success, England pip Spain as the nation with the most players, 14 to 13, followed by the USA and France with nine each, while Copa América winners Brazil move into the top five for the first time with five players of their own.

The Women’s Super League asserts its dominance with 39 players on the list, up 12 from 2024, ahead of the NWSL with 19 and Liga F with 16. Players such as Jess Park, Aoba Fujino, Mary Fowler and Maya Le Tissier just missed out.

The young and old were once again represented at either end of the spectrum, with Marta again the oldest representative, the 39-year-old playing a key role in Brazil’s Copa América success with a dramatic late goal in the final against Colombia to keep their hopes alive. Talks have started over Manchester City star Josko Gvardiol's exit from the Etihad.

That's according to one report, which says that the Croatian defender's departure may have begun as early as the summer, with the future of the Citizens uncertain and a potential points deduction coming after an independent commission found the club guilty of over a hundred charges of financial rule-breaking.

Manchester City have launched an appeal – but an exodus could well be on the way, with Gvardiol the first domino.

January isn't the optimal time for transfer business, but Barcelona have interest in Gvardiol, as per AS via Sport Witness, with Hansi Flick wanting to improve his defence if he's to land a sixth Champions League title in Catalonia this season.

The report states that the Blaugrana asked about taking the 24-year-old along with Rodri while negotiating a move for the 2024 Ballon d'Or winner – but that the deal is “almost impossible” this winter due to the La Liga champions needing to raise funds to secure a major new signing.

That's where Manchester United come into play, with the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone and having just hired Mauricio Pochettino to turn fortunes around.

United have an interest in Alejandro Balde, with the La Masia graduate failing to get the requisite playing time under Flick, and should Pochettino request a new full-back, the signing could well bolster the coffers for Barça to pursue Gvardiol.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Gvardiol is said to be wanted by Flick for his athleticism and his ability to play both centrally and at left-back, but having signed a new deal at the Etihad Stadium over the summer, he may be completely unattainable now.

City maintain their innocence over the 115 charges, but should the club face a serious penalty, Gvardiol would surely reconsider his future, despite his recent contract extension.

The Athletic have noted that RB Leipzig’s Castello Lukeba is an option for Barcelona – as is United's own Lisandro Martinez, who fell out with club hierarchy recently over comments aimed at his team's recruitment over the summer.

The same report also mentions that United made a “deadline day check” on Balde but decided not to go any further with the deal.

Gvardiol is worth €75 million, according to Transfermarkt. City face Fulham when Premier League action resumes this weekend.

Leeds United's Tarik Muharemovic ranks alongside Virgil van Dijk and Gabriel in Premier League centre-back data

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Leeds United defender Tarik Muharemovic has emerged as one of the Premier League’s most complete centre-backs this season, ranking alongside Arsenal’s Gabriel and Ezri Konsa, and Liverpool’s Virgil van Dijk.

Data published by football analytics platform Ballity Insight Lab evaluated 54 qualifying Premier League centre-backs across the opening 10 league games of 2026/27, plotting each player’s percentile rank across two criteria: front-foot 'stopper' centre-backs and the more disciplined 'covering' centre-backs.

In the model, a stopper is measured by their ability to step out of the defensive line and win the ball, encompassing tackles, aerial duels, clearances and interceptions. Conversely, a covering centre-back is judged on positional security and composure, factoring in ball retention, recoveries and an avoidance of errors.

Out of the 54 central defenders assessed, only four sit inside the top-right quadrant reserved for players who excel at both covering and stopping. Alongside established title contenders Van Dijk and Gabriel, as well as England international Konsa, sits Elland Road favourite Muharemovic.

The numbers underline just how consistently the Bosnia-Herzegovina international has performed at the heart of Leeds’ backline. Muharemovic sits comfortably around the 77th percentile in both the stopper and cover pools, demonstrating an ability to step aggressively into challenges while also sweeping up danger in transition.

Stopper or Cover? Premier League centre-backs 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 🛑 Stopper CB: steps out and wins the ball. Tackles, aerials, clearances, interceptions and duels. 🧠 Cover CB: rarely beaten and keeps the ball. Dribble avoidance, ball retention, recoveries and few errors. Formula in the comments 👇 🇳🇱 Van Dijk, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Konsa, 🇧🇷 Gabriel and 🇧🇦 Muharemović do both to some degree. 🇸🇪 Lindelöf, 🇵🇹 Dias, 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Guéhi and 🇳🇱 Van de Ven cover, but don’t stop. Needs a stopper as a partner 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Hill, 🇳🇱 Botman and 🇧🇷 Murillo stop, but don’t cover. Needs a cover as a partner.November 16, 2026

He keeps elite company at the top end of the chart with Liverpool skipper Van Dijk still leading the cover metric near the 98th percentile while posting around an 80th-percentile stopper score.

Konsa hovers near the 92nd percentile for covering and 88th for stopping, and Arsenal’s Gabriel posts roughly 83rd-percentile marks across both categories.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Just as striking is the calibre of Premier League defenders who fall outside that dual-threat bracket. Several household names are classified as being better covering central defenders than stoppers, meaning they thrive at reading the game and keeping possession, but rely on a more aggressive partner to engage attackers directly.

Manchester City’s Ruben Dias and Marc Guehi, as well as Tottenham Hotspur’s Micky van de Ven all fall into that zone.

Muharemovic’s capacity to bridge both roles has proven invaluable for Leeds so far this season, and the Whites have established themselves as a tricky team to beat.

Whether it be winning first contacts against physical Premier League strikers or dropping off to snuff out balls over the top, the Bosnian's balanced skillset allows Leeds to pair him flexibly across their central defensive trio.

In a division where most central defenders lean heavily toward one side of the game, rubbing shoulders with Van Dijk and Gabriel is a ringing endorsement of Muharemovic’s rapid acclimatisation at Elland Road.

Muharemovic is valued at £33.3 million by Transfermarkt.

#1045. Microbiome home tests are taking off. Can they be trusted?

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Amber Dance is a freelance science writer near Los Angeles, California.

A mix of microorganisms from a human faecal sample, imaged using a scanning electron microscope. Credit: Steve Gschmeissner/Science Photo Library

First, the good news: I have 133 microbial species living in my gut. That’s a collection that ranks as ‘excellent’ according to NirvanaBiome, the company in Germantown, Maryland, that analysed my stool sample. The firm based its rating on the overall diversity of my gut’s residents plus my levels of specific beneficial and undesirable species.

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

Revealed: how this common gut microbe protects against heart disease

But then came a second, less promising assessment: Viome in Bellevue, Washington, identified only 61 kinds of active microorganism in my gut and suggested that some of them were not performing optimally. Viome recommended dietary changes and offered customized supplements to improve my health.

I was intrigued by the results, but also flummoxed by the different messages. That’s not an uncommon response, says microbiologist Rob Knight, director of the Center for Microbiome Innovation at the University of California, San Diego. When scientists tested a handful of microbiome testing kits alongside one another in formal studies, they found wide discrepancies in the results. These differences make it hard to understand or really trust the findings from any given provider, says Diane Hoffmann, director of the Law and Health Care programme at the University of Maryland in Baltimore, who co-authored one of those studies.

The companies stand by their products. “Of course there’s variability,” says Kelly Moffat, chief operations officer for Cmbio in Germantown, which does the laboratory work and genetic sequencing for NirvanaBiome. “There has to be because this is complex testing.”

Momo Vuyisich, chief science officer at Viome’s lab in Bothwell, Washington, also says he was unsurprised by the degree of variation found by formal studies. Labs use different methods to extract, sequence and analyse microbial genetic material. Viome, for example, sequences RNA rather than DNA, allowing it to uncover microbial gene activity, rather than only the presence of genes. Vuyisich argues that this is more relevant to human health. And he says that although every method will have biases, as long as a consumer sticks with the same provider, it should produce results that are comparable over time.

Interest in these kinds of test is booming. “There’s so much public enthusiasm and excitement about the microbiome,” says Knight. Some customers are simply curious about the microscopic beings that live inside them and potentially affect their health; others have health conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and hope that their gut microbes will reveal the underlying cause or a path to better health.

Although people can order the tests and follow their recommendations without the help of a medical professional, some people are bringing the findings to their physicians. “I groan when I see someone come in with a microbiome test,” says Fergus Shanahan, a gastroenterologist and immunologist at University College Cork in Ireland, who has spent much of his career studying the microbiome. For someone struggling with gut health, a consumer microbiome profile isn’t usually specific enough to help. And if there’s a concern about an infection, such as Clostridioides difficile, it’s more straightforward to test for known pathogens than to assess the entire microbial community.

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

The tantalizing links between gut microbes and the brain

Microbiologists and gasteroenterologists who spoke to Nature generally agreed that microbiome testing has the potential to both reflect and promote health, but many said that the science isn’t yet mature enough to support microbiome testing for most consumers. In their view, the limited clinical usefulness of today’s consumer tests can make them poor value for money (costing around US$100–300). The specialists warn that acting on advice that doesn’t come from clinicians could lead customers to adopt unnecessarily restrictive diets or delay appropriate medical assessment. Critics say that consumer microbiome testing needs more regulatory scrutiny and oversight.

“This is an industry that’s running wild,” says genomicist Jacques Ravel, director of the Center for Advanced Microbiome Research and Innovation at the University of Maryland School of Medicine in Baltimore and a co-author on one of the studies that tested several providers. With regards to testing methods, he says, “there’s no standard”.

Moffat says, “I think the jury’s out on exactly what it is that we can actionably do today based on this data.” But she says that microbiome profiles, combined with other testing such as gut metabolomics, could yield interesting and useful health information.

The gut microbiome has emerged as an incredible correlate of overall health. From immune-system function to metabolism, skin disorders and mental health, study after study has found links between a person’s well-being and the trillions of microbes that live in their digestive tract. The premise of a head count of these species and assessment of their actions, to monitor and improve gut health in a personalized way, certainly sounds appealing. Viome’s website, for example, promises: “No more trial and error … Follow a plan built precisely for you.”

Companies can identify species and, on the basis of those lists, infer what the microbes are probably doing, such as manufacturing metabolites or inciting inflammation. But running even the simplest microbiome testing is expensive, says Alessandra Cervino, research director at PiLeJe, a science-based food-supplement company in Paris. She says her microbiome testing company, Luxia Scientific, closed in 2024 for financial reasons.

Some microbiome testing firms recommend fermented foods, such as kombucha, for gut health.Credit: Deb Lindsey for The Washington Post via Getty

Many testing companies also offer lifestyle and nutritional advice or sell supplements. For example, Viome analysed diverse functions performed by the microbes in my gut, such as digestive efficiency, gas production and serotonin manufacture. I then received a detailed eating plan — which told me to eschew broccoli and load up on pecans, among other suggestions — along with an offer for precision supplements and probiotics with a price tag of more than $150 a month. Although it’s hard to change the composition of microbes in one’s gut, alterations in diet or even simply ageing can shift their activities, says Vuyisich. The company recommends re-testing every four to six months to check for shifts and update the plan.

He points to 19 peer-reviewed publications by Viome as evidence of the company’s rigour (see go.nature.com/4actdhq). For example, the firm’s analysis for consumers is supported, in part, by published data on how gut microbes influence individuals’ responses to glucose in various foods, based on 550 people in the United States who collectively ate more than 30,000 meals while wearing glucose monitors1. The company validated those findings in a further cohort in Japan, Vuyisich says, but those data are not published.

Microbiome tests are not created equal, says Tim Spector, a physician-scientist at King’s College London and co-founder of London-based ZOE, which offers microbiome testing and a supplement in addition to a gut-health app that I’ve been playing with. ZOE’s products, Spector says, are backed by research on thousands of people. “There definitely are some not-so-good players out there that give this field a bad name,” he says. “It’s not easy to do this well.”

There are also several ways to do microbe testing; companies take varying approaches that yield disparate results, as at least two studies have shown. Scientists at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Gaithersburg, Maryland, shipped homogenized stool samples from one person to seven companies2. NIST’s remit is researching and applying standards for measurement. This experiment was a step towards understanding the diversity of testing options out there, says one of the study authors, NIST microbiologist Stephanie Servetas, who is based in Sheridan, Wyoming. The researchers didn’t name the companies in their report because they wanted to focus attention on the comparison between tests rather than perceived accuracy of any individual provider.

The result: “Companies produce strikingly different results,” says co-author Scott Jackson, a molecular geneticist who used to direct the NIST microbiology program and is now a consultant in Saint Michaels, Maryland. “They couldn’t even agree on what’s healthy and unhealthy,” Jackson says. The microbe lists ranged from 34 to 906 identified genera; only 3 of which showed up in all reports. In fact, the results were as varied from company to company as they would be for different people, despite all tests being done on samples from the same individual.

A European and Canadian team obtained similar outcomes when they sent homogenized samples from one person’s stool to six companies, also anonymized. Three companies rated the microbial diversity as “excellent” or “good”; two called it “average”; one said it was “unfavourable”3. The results were so variable, that at least some of them must be lacking in validation or standardization, says co-author Céline Druart, executive director of the Pharmabiotic Research Institute (PRI) in Brussels, a non-profit organization specializing in regulation of microbiome innovations. “It’s very difficult to make a conclusion,” she says.

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

How gut bacteria could boost cancer treatments

This broad divergence in results is not surprising, says Jack Gilbert, director of the Microbiome and Metagenomics Center at the University of California, San Diego. The variation starts at sampling: scoop a bit of faecal matter into a tube, stab it with a coring device or swipe the sampler across some used toilet paper; ship it off as-is, or in some kind of preservative (as both Viome’s and NirvanaBiome’s kits asked me to). Each option could influence the balance of the microbes that are collected and what survives to be sequenced.

In the lab, Servetas says the method by which the researchers extract genetic material from a sample is a big source of divergence. Gentler protocols will bias a sample towards microbes that are easy to crack open, whereas harsher methods will capture a higher share of species with tougher exteriors.

After sequencing, another major source of difference, says Knight, is the bioinformatics pipeline that labs use. What length or number of genetic sequences is required to consider a microbe present? What list of sequences and microbes are they using as a reference? “All bets are off when you then computationally analyse it with your favourite method,” says Knight.

Would companies support having standards to validate their tests? “We are really big advocates on really having a standard here,” says Kimberley Sukhum, chief science officer at Tiny Health in Austin, Texas, which offers gut microbiome tests as well as vaginal microbiome tests.

But it’s hard to set those standards, in part because there is no known ‘ground truth’ for a natural microbial sample. Compare that with, say, a blood-glucose test; a lab can get a known value from a standard sample either right or wrong. But the microbiome, in its glorious complexity, does not allow for such simple validation. NIST has used mixed human donor samples to develop a standard4. And Tiny Health has experimented with generating a reference for benchmarking from synthetic communities. It was built from individual microbial species rather than sampled from faeces5. But neither of those standards is exactly like the microbiome of an individual person.

Even if labs could assess a microbiome perfectly, they’d still have a problem: there’s no defined healthy microbiome like there is one range of healthy blood-glucose levels. Each person’s microbiome is unique, like a fingerprint. There are infinitely many ways to have a healthy microbiome, and infinitely many ways to have an unhealthy one, says Shanahan; it’s not entirely clear how to draw a line between the two.

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

How gut microbes could drive brain disorders

Companies must compare customer microbiomes with some standard of health, but these vary too. They might be based on past customers or large, public databases. But microbiomes differ considerably depending on factors such as ethnicity, sex, age, recent antibiotic use or even whether someone was born by caesarean section.

#1044. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#1042. Germany news: Merz hopes for Korean reunification at DMZ

Chancellor Friedrich Merz has expressed hope for Korean reunification during a visit to the heavily fortified border. Meanwhile, President Steinmeier has held talks with China's Xi Jinping in Beijing.

Below, you can review the leading headlines from and about Germany from Friday, October 30:

Chancellor Friedrich Merz visits the demilitarized zone between North and South Korea

Merz draws on Germany's own reunification experience, saying division causes suffering

Two German leaders, two parallel missions across Asia.

While President Frank-Walter Steinmeier sought to reinforce ties with China in Beijing, Chancellor Friedrich Merz toured Japan, South Korea and Singapore, promoting closer cooperation among what he calls the world's "middle powers."

Together, the visits highlight Berlin's effort to lower risks without decoupling from China.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany's annual inflation rate eased to 2.8% in October from 3.3% in September, with economists pointing to the government's fuel tax cut as the main reason.

Preliminary figures from the Federal Statistical Office showed energy prices rose 12.2% compared with a year earlier, down from 14.9% in September. Services inflation slowed to 2.5%, while food inflation remained at 0.4%.

"The decisive factor was the fuel tax cut," said Silke Tober of the Macroeconomic Policy Institute. The reduction took effect in October and runs through December, although rising crude oil prices partly offset the savings at the pump.

ING bank economist Carsten Brzeski said higher energy costs had yet to feed through into broader price increases. Unlike during the 2022 energy crisis, consumers were unwilling or unable to absorb substantially higher prices, he said.

But economists warned the relief could prove temporary. "Gas and oil prices have risen significantly again in recent weeks," said Stephanie Schoenwald, an economist at Germany's state-owned development bank KfW, citing continuing conflicts and lower inventories.

German President's Frank-Walter Steinmeier latest trip to Asia was intended to provide more clarity. Amid a delicate period, Steinmeier sought a balancing act in China between respect and criticism.

It was a state visit of a kind rarely seen today. For four days, Steinmeier traveled across the country: from Hefei, where the German automaker Volkswagen's China operations are headquartered, through historic villages and the imposing landscapes of the Yellow Mountains. He also visited several points of interest of Chinese history, art, and science, and finally, he headed to Tiananmen Square in the heart of Beijing's political center.

Steinmeier—who is set to leave office in March 2027— spoke as a statesman and diplomat on matters of German and European interest. Chinese President Xi Jinping and Steinmeier have known each other for many years, so in this respect, the president was the right man to address even the most difficult issues as a European.

This political balancing act between respect and criticism did not trigger any visible outrage in Beijing.

When he spoke with Chinese leaders about their subsidies for exports to Europe and the related issue of the trade deficit, Xi replied: "I am ready to work together to open a new chapter in the comprehensive strategic partnership between our two countries and to advance the development of global governance."

Just how much willingness lies behind the push for a strategic partnership will become clear during further negotiations between the EU and China.

Xi Jinping seems to understand that a persistent trade deficit with Europe could also become a problem for his country, as an economic crisis in Europe could further strain China's economy.

As "the world's second- and third-largest economies," China and Germany also bear "an important responsibility for the development of relations between China and Europe, as well as for stable growth in the global economy," Xi Jinping said. While that may not sound like a breakthrough yet, it certainly sounds like an understanding.

In contrast to his economic arguments, Steinmeier's political appeals for Beijing to assume more responsibility for the international order fell on deaf ears.

The German president addressed global conflicts and wars on several occasions in Beijing, including Russia's war of aggression in Ukraine. But he received no responses in official statements.

That same evening, the news channel of the Chinese TV network CCTV aired a report that merely covered Steinmeier's visit to a well-known astrophysics institute.

There was no mention of the call for China, as a permanent member of the UN Security Council, to do more to promote world peace.

Mitat Özdemir is one of more than 870,000 Turkish workers who were recruited to Germany by a government program between 1961 and 1973. He dealt with tough factory work, language barriers and cultural differences.

Six decades later, he and his family still live in Germany. How did the program from back then shape their lives and modern Germany?

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday visited the Panmunjom truce village at the demilitarized zone (DMZ) separating North and South Korea, briefly standing on the North Korean side inside the barracks.

North and South Korea have been divided since the end of hostilities in the Korean War in 1953, with a border running across the peninsula.

In remarks to reporters, Merz recalled Germany's reunification 36 years ago.

"Let us hope that Korea too gets the chance one day to regain state unity," he said.

"You can also notice it here at this place, how much a country suffers from division and how strong the desire is for reunification, at least in this part of the Korean Peninsula," he said, adding that he had been asked about Germany's reunification experience while visiting Seoul.

North Korea, however, has backed away in recent years from diplomacy with the South, having officially removed language calling for reunification from its constitution while changing the South's status to that of a "hostile state."

A glass cabinet containing memorabilia linked to the 1958 Munich Air Disaster, in which eight Manchester United footballers lost their lives, was smashed and plundered in the Munich suburb of Trudering this week.

The display case on Manchesterplatz forms part of a memorial commemorating the tragedy which occurred when the United team made a refueling stop in Munich while on the way back from a European Cup game in Belgrade, Serbia, on February 6, 1958.

The plane struggled to take off again in the wintery conditions at the old Munich-Riem airport to the east of the city center and, on the third attempt, ploughed off the end of the runway and into a house. Of the 44 people on board, 23 were killed, including eight United players, several journalists and two crew members.

The crash site has become a place of pilgrimage for United supporters and, in 2020, the cabinet was installed on the initiative of the Red Docs Munich – a local Bayern Munich fan club – to house the various memorabilia and tributes left by visitors.

Munich police said the cabinet was broken into on Monday morning between 8 a.m. and 1 p.m. local time (07:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. UTC), with the unknown perpetrators making off with a glass sculpture and several medals.

"They don't understand the damage that they've caused," Ifty Ahmed, chairman of the Manchester Munich Memorial Foundation (MMMF), told the BBC, adding: "Whatever they've taken from inside the showcase, they haven't taken our memories."

The Red Docs Munich arranged for replacement glass to be installed on the same day. The MMMF said Manchester United had offered to pay for the repairs but said the foundation had covered the costs itself.

The joint commemoration of the 1958 disaster and the maintenance of the memorial site has produced extensive and friendly relations between Bayern Munich and Manchester United, who will meet in the Champions League in January.

German politicians have been slow to respond as they wait to see who is likely to comprise the next coalition. Many are also hoping for a government without religious hardliners.

Profits of German luxury car brand Audi for the third quarter came plunged 87% year-on-year to €95 million ($106 million), the Volkswagen subsidiary reported on Friday. This is a drop from €718 million seen in the same quarter last year.

The drop comes amid weak demand in China, and US tariffs.

"Market and competitive conditions have become significantly more difficult in the third quarter," Audi chief financial officer Jürgen Rittersberger told journalists on a call.

"That all shows that we need to intensify measures and set clear priorities," he added.

Overall in the first nine months of 2026, Audi's profits have dropped 41% to €1.22 billion.

The carmaker trimmed its 2026 profit outlook down to 3 to 5% for the year, down from the previous 5 to 7%.

Audi's sluggish numbers represent more bad news for the 10-brand Volkswagen Group, which on Thursday reported its largest quarterly loss in more than a ‌decade, at nearly €6 billion.

A ban on new Stolpersteine ("stumbling stones") to commemorate victims of the Holocaust in the eastern German town of Heidenau will be upheld after five petitions against the measure were thrown out.

Local councilors from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) voted together in September to pass the controversial ban on new stones being laid in the town in Saxony, near Dresden.

Petitions against the measure were submitted from across Germany — as well as one from the Netherlands — calling for victims of the Nazi regime to continue to be remembered in Heidenau by way of the small metal plaques embedded in pavements.

"Not everybody has to like the stumbling stones but everyone should have the possibility to lay one in public," one councilor, Michael Schürer, told Germany's Catholic News Agency (KNA), criticizing the rejection of the petitions.

The initiators of the Heidenau ban had argued that, while remembering Holocaust victims remains essential, the placement of Stolpersteine leads to "passersby walking over or even stepping onto the names of the victims." They suggested honoring victims at a local cemetery instead.

The decision of the local Heidenau CDU to join forces with the AfD to pass the motion sparked a nationwide scandal and furthered the debate over the conservatives' commitment to the political "firewall" against the far right.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ahead of talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Friday, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier lauded China's role as a global technological and economic power, while emphasizing the responsibility that comes along with it.

"We both bear responsibility for the ⁠international order ​and for the conditions under which states in this world maintain and shape their relations," Steinmeier said.

President Xi praised what he called an "all-dimensional strategic partnership" between China and Germany, calling for new cooperation based on stability and mutual benefit.

"This new paradigm sends a positive signal to the world: we favor openness over closure, and cooperation over confrontation," Xi said during opening remarks, emphasizing the start of a "new chapter" in Germany-China ties.

Xi added that he hopes Germany and the European Union will stick by a "rational, pragmatic and friendly" China policy, adding that cooperation outweighs competition and consensus outweighs differences in China-EU relations.

The EU has a massive trade deficit with China, which reached €360 billion ($400.4 billion) last year and is set to exceed that level this year.

Brussels has accused China of unfair economic practices, saying its state subsidies for its industries are creating an unlevel playing field. Germany with its export based economy, the EU's largest, is hit hard by China's manufacturing surplus flooding global markets.

Industry groups say the surge in imports from China is leading to an increasing number of factory closures in the bloc.

Nonetheless, "differences and problems can always be resolved," the Chinese president said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

On October 30, 1961, West Germany and Turkey signed an agreement allowing the temporary recruitment of workers. Sixty-five years on, many so-called "guest workers" cannot live from their pensions.

Learn more about how "guest workers" are struggling as they reach retirement age in this in depth report by Oliver Pieper.

While German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in South Korea on Friday called for a better rule-based trade order, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier was in the Chinese capital in a bid to smooth out trade disagreements.

In Beijing, Steinmeier called for preserving the "win-win principle" characterizing Sino-German relations, borrowing from the expression "win-win cooperation," one of the most frequently used phrases in Chinese foreign policy statements.

Germany's economic ties with China have gone through a shock in recent years, with Chinese manufacturing growing into sectors once dominated by German firms, and Chinese electric cars taking over market share.

At the start of a meeting with Chinese Premier Li Qiang, Steinmeier cited a recent deal limiting exports of Chinese hybrid cars to the EU in exchange for select tariff cuts on EU exports to China as an example of a "a way to find solutions."

Steinmeier also brought up Germany's growing trade deficit with China, which grew to nearly €90 billion ($100 billion) last year.

Germany has long resisted tougher action against China, fearing retaliation. But rising pressure on key industries has pushed Berlin to seek stronger EU trade-defense powers to protect its industrial base.

Steinmeier said Germany would work to solve trade problems with China. "We are coming with the intention of maintaining and strengthening the framework for good economic exchange between our two countries," Steinmeier said.

Later in the day, the German president, who occupies a largely ceremonial role without policymaking power, was also recieved by an honor guard alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping.

During his final day of a whirlwind Asia tour this week, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told the Asia-Pacific Conference of German Business in Seoul on Friday that Germany and Europe are ready to cooperate with Asian economies to foster a rules-based economic order.

Merz said the European Union is ready to take the lead in shaping a better deal for countries in Asia feeling the pressure of a destabilized rules-based trade order.

"Competition between the US and China is ramping up. Tariffs, technological decoupling strategies and a tough race for critical raw materials and new technologies are fundamentally changing the rules of our global economy," Merz said.

"These conflicts and systemic shifts in power patterns concern us all. They particularly concern economically aspiring partners in the Indo-Pacific, as well as in Germany and in Europe."

During stops in Singapore and Japan this week, Merz pushed for free trade partnerships and greater European cooperation with Asian economies.

In Singapore on Wednesday, Merz called for a free trade agreement between the EU and the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), a sweeping multilateral free trade agreement connecting the Asia Pacific and the Americas.

The UK is the single European signatory, albeit outside of the EU bloc. The US pulled out during the first administration President Donald Trump in 2017, scuttling the original version, the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP).

"We want to offer opportunities beyond bilateral agreements,"he said in Seoul on Friday.

"We are resolutely joining forces against unilateralism, autocratic power politics and violations of international law," Merz added.

"When supply chains become political pawns, when access to key technologies is obstructed or when efforts to secure raw materials resemble displays of power rather than fair partnerships, this jeopardizes growth, prosperity and ultimately the security of entire regions."

Merz also tried to allay concerns about EU protectionism under the "Made in Europe" scheme intended to protect carmakers.

"There is a fear that we might be facing ‌a new wave of European protectionism - that we are closing ‌ourselves off from other nations," ‌Merz said.

"I take these concerns very seriously. I will carry them back not just to Berlin, ‌but also to Brussels, and I will certainly raise the fact that these concerns were expressed to me quite forcefully here," he added.

Citing Germany as an example, South Korean Prime Minister Han Seong Sook told the conference  "German companies are using Korea as a central hub to expand their presence in the Asia-Pacific region."

The question of who should become Germany's new president is becoming pressing.

Many want to see Germany's first female head of state. Chancellor Friedrich Merz is keeping his cards close to his chest.

Germany's chancellor and president were both in Asia this week, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz calling for more robust trade ties with middle powers and President Frank-Walter Steinmeier focusing on diplomacy   during a multi-day visit to China.

On Friday, Merz spoke at a German-South Korean business conference in Seoul, while Steinmeier is set to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

England want to host the Nations League, but things are never easy hosting international football in this country

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Football Association has registered interest in England hosting the Nations League finals.

On Sunday, the Three Lions booked their place as one of the top seeds in the newly expanded quarter-finals of the competition, beating world champions Spain to set up a clash against a second seed in March.

And England could well be playing a semi on home soil, if the FA has anything to do with it.

According to Sami Mokbel of the BBC, England, Spain and France have all contacted UEFA, expressing their desire to host the final four games of next summer's Nations League competition.

The competition began in 2019, with the inaugural finals both hosted and ultimately won by Portugal, before heading to Italy (2021), the Netherlands (2023), and, most recently, Germany (2025).

England will face one of Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark or Norway in the last eight of the competition – and could well become the first host of the finals not to reach the final four, given the new format of the competition.

So far, the only publically announced events at Wembley this June are two concerts from Newcastle United fan, Sam Fender, though these are scheduled to take place after the Nations League is due to be played.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

FourFourTwo understands that the FA would welcome the opportunity to host a mini-tournament with the European Championship coming to the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland in 2028 – with other venues in consideration for hosting duties next summer.

While the Etihad Stadium is booked for much of June for Oasis's Live '27 tour, the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium is, so far, free to host, with cult noughties emo band Fall Out Boy and stadium rock veterans U2 booked either side of when the semi-finals would take place.

The Hill Dickinson Stadium in Liverpool, meanwhile, could well host its first major internationals.

This isn't a new conundrum for the FA to solve, with the Community Shield recently affected by Wembley's commitments beyond football.

This summer, the season's curtain-raiser was held in Cardiff at the Millennium Stadium, while 2022 saw Erling Haaland make his Manchester City debut at the King Power Stadium in the fixture.

England will play home and away in the next international break in the Nations League quarter.

#1037. Which football club has had most international captains in the same team? | The Knowledge

Plus: more speedy marathons by footballers, headed goals of the season and chairs acting as managers

Mail us with all of your questions and answers

“Which club team has had the most international captains playing together at one time?” asks MH Zahid. “Conversely, which international team has had the most club captains in its starting lineup at one time?”

A quick web search finds a fuss being made in various corners of the internet of Chelsea’s 2009-10 squad because it contained six national team captains in Michael Ballack (Germany), Petr Cech (Czech Republic), Didier Drogba (Côte d’Ivoire), Branislav Ivanovic (Serbia), Mikel John Obi (Nigeria) and John Terry (England). These are, indeed, six people who captained their countries, playing together at one time, but crucially they were not all international captains at that time, which because we like to have our hands bound as tight as possible – no questions please – mean they are disqualified from this particular tournament. Ivanovic, you see, was not named Serbia captain until 2012 and Mikel, who was but a whippersnapper at 22 when the 2009-10 season started, was still seven years from getting his hands on the Nigeria armband.

But if that Chelsea team are not themselves the best answer that Knowledge has come up with, they are at least associated with them, having been knocked out of the Champions League by José Mourinho’s captain-strewn Inter. Inter ended up beating Bayern Munich 2-0 in the final, with a team that included the then full-time captains of Brazil (Lúcio), Romania (Cristian Chivu), Cameroon (Samuel Eto’o) and Macedonia (Goran Pandev), while the captain of Serbia (Dejan Stankovic) came off the bench to replace Chivu in the second half and Pandev was replaced by Sulley Muntari, who while not Ghana’s full-time captain had led the side in their most recent game, a 2-1 defeat at Bosnia and Herzegovina that March.

But that’s not all! Among the unused substitutes was Iván Córdoba, who at this point in his career had lost Colombia’s armband to Mario Yepes but been given it back for their previous game, against Paraguay, in the absence of his fellow centre-back. Also in the team and worthy of note, if not of inclusion in our tally of then captains, were Wesley Sneijder, occasional Netherlands skipper and still their all-time record appearance maker, and Javier Zanetti, who regularly captained Argentina and is No 4 on their list of all-time appearance makers (he would be higher had he not been frozen out by their then manager, Diego Maradona, before the 2010 World Cup), with occasional Kenya captain McDonald Mariga also among the subs.

By our count that’s seven players in one matchday squad who could boast of being their country’s current captain at kick-off, and none of whom captained their club side – that honour went to Zanetti. Our searches have not found another team to match that one, but readers have suggested a couple who came close, in the shape of Tottenham in 2020-21 (who boasted five international captains at the time in Hugo Lloris of France; Serge Aurier of Côte d’Ivoire; South Korea’s Son Heung-min; Gareth Bale of Wales; and England’s own Harry Kane, suggested by John Curry) and Liverpool just last year, when in Conor Bradley, Andy Robertson, Virgil van Dijk, Wataru Endo, Mo Salah and Dominik Szoboszlai they had six – though they never played together while they were all incumbent international captains. Any more for any more?

The fastest former footballer we found in time for last week’s instalment was Alexei Smertin, the former Russia and Chelsea midfielder, who screamed around the Kazan Marathon course in 2020 in just two hours, 48 minutes and 17 seconds. But as Richard Askham emailed to point out, that has since been bettered by Joe Skarz, formerly of Bury, Rotherham and Oxford United, and current manager of Golcar United of the Northern Counties East League Premier Division, who in 2025 finished the Yorkshire Marathon with a chip time of 2hr 47min 33sec.

The next question is what level of football do you need to reach to qualify as a footballer? Because Stig Lindmark tipped us off about the former AIK academy player Andreas Almgren, whose dreams of football glory were derailed by injury in his teens and eventually shifted his focus towards distance running. In New York at the start of this month – while the retired cyclist Tom Dumoulin was putting most former footballers to shame with a time of 2:27:12 – he ran his first ever marathon and only went and won the thing, in 2hr 6min 1sec. With no senior competitive appearances he probably does not count, but it’s a good enough effort to get a mention.

“Has a headed goal ever been awarded goal of the season,” wonders Rupert Sheard. “I can think of a few belters, but awards tend to go to ones kicked in.”

“The closest I could get was Robin van Persie’s flying header at the 2014 World Cup in Brazil, for the Netherlands against Spain,” writes Sinan Eccles. “He was pipped to the official goal of the tournament by James Rodríguez’s iconic volley, but did make it to third in that year’s Puskas Award – behind Rodríguez and Stephanie Roche.”

Peter Tomlin writes: “Having researched the goal of the season awards in many countries, the only header I could find that won was Keith Houchen’s fantastic one in the 1986-87 FA Cup Final for Coventry v Tottenham. However, Alisson’s dramatic 95th-minute headed winner v West Brom was voted Liverpool’s goal of the season for the 2020-21 season.”

And Mark Johnson points out that Basile Boli’s ridiculous bullet header for Marseille against PSG at the end of the 1993 season would surely have won the Ligue 1 goal of the season award but for the inconvenient fact that no such award existed at the time.

Martyn Amos has responded to last week’s scepticism about the possibility of an Ipswich fan website existing in 1990, the year before the first known website went online. “Just to clarify, the original page was set up by Phil Clarke, who was working at BT Labs in Martlesham (near Ipswich), in 1990,” he writes. “At the time, as I said, the web was still experimental, and I think the page was only available internally. Your correspondent is correct in saying that the first public website appeared in August 1991. But the ITFC page still existed, in some recognisable form, using the standard web technology, in 1990, so I think it counts. That’s my understanding, anyway.”

With Lee Power taking charge of Swindon Town, in last week’s Knowledge archive we dug up our piece from 2006 on chairs acting as managers, we wrote in October 2015. Neil Bellis, the director of communications at Chester FC, writes to point out we missed Terry Smith off our list.

“He took over four games into the season despite not really knowing much about ‘soccer’,” writes Neil. “He was a former American Football coach but for some reason ending up buying our club. Not only did we end up getting relegated from the Football League for the first time in 1999-2000 we also saw a few very strange ideas from him including having a team talk as the Lord’s prayer and appointing a captain in defence, midfield and attack. Thankfully we are now fan owned so this level of insanity shouldn’t happen again.”

One of Smith’s first games as manager was against Aston Villa in the League Cup, a fixture that prompted a visit from ITV to see what was going on. The result of that visit can be seen here:

“There’s nothing magical about being a coach,’ said Smith not long after his arrival. “It’s like being the general manager of a business, the coaching principles are the same in any sport.” That doesn’t sound too promising but things didn’t really go horribly wrong until the end of November, when Chester began a run of 11 defeats in 12 matches. There’s some footage here of the aftermath of the 5-1 home defeat by Leyton Orient just after Christmas – “I want to thank you guys,” says Smith in the dressing room. “That’s the most pitiful, pitiful effort I’ve ever damn seen.”

Smith stepped down as manager and brought in Ian Atkins in January 2000, then sold the club in October 2001.

“What’s the highest score by a team or in a match where no player scored more than one goal?” writes Paul Gage.

“Manchester United have 20 league titles, won by three managers. Liverpool have 20 league titles won by 10. Which teams have the most and fewest titles won by the most and fewest managers?” asks Will Marquand.

“Djed Spence (shirt No 99) set up Pio Esposito (No 94) in Inter’s 2-0 win over Como at the weekend. Has there ever been a combination for a goal (assist and scorer) with a higher combined shirt number than 193?” writes Joe Strawson.

“Did the Fenerbahce side have more combined Premier League appearances than Liverpool in the teams’ recent Champions League match? If so was this the first instance of a club in Europe playing opposition who had more game appearances in their own league than they had themselves?” ponders Josh Wolff-Martin.

#1035. WSL talking points: Chelsea’s gamble pays off and have Arsenal lost fear factor?

Blues beat champions after bold substitution and Gunners’ home struggles continue with fifth consecutive WSL draw

Sonia Bompastor attempted to deflect suggestions that the removal of Kadeisha Buchanan 12 minutes into Chelsea’s top-of-the-table clash with Manchester City was tactical, but few were convinced by the claim that it was down to injury. The manager said the centre-back, who had not asked to come off and walked straight down the tunnel, had taken a knock to the head in training and been assessed and cleared, but that during the game “she was not herself”. On came Veerle Buurman and the threat of Khadija Shaw was nullified, the Dutch defender restricting the golden boot favourite so well that Shaw did not manage a shot on target. Bompastor said after the game that she had not spoken to Buchanan but that she would “explain myself to her”. “I always have good relationships with the players, bring them clarity, and I’m always direct and honest so they have the information,” she said. “It won’t be any different.” Enforced or not, the substitution was a huge gamble that paid off, even after the loss of Melvine Malard to injury in the first half reduced their number of remaining in-game substitution windows to one. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-0 Manchester City

Manchester United earned their fourth clean sheet in all competitions in their 2-0 defeat of Crystal Palace. Maya Le Tissier stole the headlines with her goal on her 150th appearance for the club but the team’s improved defensive stability is also catching the eye and the centre-back is key to that. “For a defender you expect as the minimum you need to defend well and help to build,” said the head coach, Eva Olid. “But now she’s scoring goals and that is more than a manager can ask from a centre-back. She’s in a high level and I’m so happy for her.” Le Tissier is showing consistent solidity and appears to be enjoying life under Olid now that things have settled, after seven goals conceded in their opening two WSL games. United have conceded four in eight WSL games since and are starting to show their flair. SW

Have teams stopped fearing Arsenal at the Emirates Stadium? Their run of five consecutive WSL draws at home suggests so. London City Lionesses had 56% possession on Sunday and controlled the game for significant spells, especially in the second half, and although Arsenal created the greater chances, they do not play with the aura of a side attracting the largest attendances in the division. Renée Slegers was asked whether she was worried her team were losing that home “fear factor” and said: “No, because we love playing at the Emirates. We had the biggest crowd so far in the season, the atmosphere was fantastic under the lights.” Probed further about her side’s home form, the head coach said: “I don’t think we’ve lost the fear factor, I think it’s a very hard place for oppositions to come.” Her side host West Ham next Sunday, looking for that elusive home WSL win. Tom Garry

Tottenham Hotspur were the latest team frustrated by Everton’s defensive solidity as they were held to a goalless draw. Despite controlling the ball and registering 17 shots, only three efforts were on target as they failed to score for the first time. Martin Ho was keen to highlight their opponents’ strengths as a key reason. “When we got into that attacking third, it was going to take something really special,” he told Spursplay. “They defended so deep with so many numbers behind the ball. You’re waiting for one of those moments to drop.” It was just the kind of performance fans have come to expect from Scott Phelan’s side. Unbeaten in their past three, in which they have faced Manchester United, Chelsea and Spurs, Everton have developed a strong resilience and character in recent weeks. Where they struggle is at the other end. Everton have scored eight goals this season (three of them own goals), higher than only Charlton in the WSL. Sophie Downey

Liverpool ended their five-game winless league run with a statement victory over struggling Brighton, their third away win in 17 games. It has been a frustrating October and November block for Gareth Taylor and his team so there was much relief on the sideline that they were finally able to turn performance and opportunity into three points. Liverpool had less of the ball but their fast counterattacking proved too much for the Seagulls. A significant key to their success was Beata Olsson. She has six goals from her past five games in all competitions, stepping up when her team have needed it most. Injuries have kept out Aurélie Csillag and Ceri Holland for the best part of the season and Sophie Roman Haug is recovering from an anterior cruciate ligament injury sustained 13 months ago. With limited attacking options, therefore, it will be very welcome that the Swedish striker has found her form in front of goal. SD

Viviane Asseyi continued her impressive scoring form with a superb brace in West Ham’s 2-0 victory over Charlton, taking her WSL tally to seven this season. The striker opened the scoring with a composed finish from the edge of the area before producing the standout moment of the afternoon, curling a spectacular 25-yard free-kick into the top corner beyond Charlton’s goalkeeper, Anna Koivunen. Asseyi could have completed a hat-trick but her two goals proved decisive. West Ham’s head coach, Rita Guarino, described her as “an important player”, adding that Asseyi was in a good goalscoring spell. Guarino felt Asseyi could have been happier with a hat-trick, but her latest double underlines her importance to West Ham’s attacking threat. Mitul Samji

Poor officiating dominated the narrative of the second city derby as Aston Villa edged Birmingham City 1-0, with both sides feeling hard done by. First, City felt Lucy Parker had fouled Océane Hurtré in the penalty area in the 24th minute, only for the referee to award a corner. Whether the incident was inside the box was disputable, but it did appear to be a foul. Minutes later, Villa had a goal from Océane Deslandes overruled for what was declared a foul on the goalkeeper in another contentious call, but they managed to find a winner in the second half. The decisions added to growing concerns about consistency in the WSL. Ho recently suggested officiating had worsened, and matches such as this do little to ease those concerns. Before VAR is introduced, improving the quality of refereeing must be a priority to avoid undermining the league’s standards and progress. Réshma Rao
