Luke Humphries suffered a last-leg 10-9 loss to debutant Tom Sykes in the second round of the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton.

It is the second big shock in the space of two days following world No 1 Luke Littler's loss to Jermaine Wattimena. Now, with the world No 2 also out, the competition is well and truly blown wide open.

Humphries looked to be struggling with a problem in his shoulder throughout the contest but managed to find some strong darts to take the contest all the way.

But Sykes, who is now ranked 72nd in the world, held on and prevailed to pick up the biggest win of his career and reach his first ever major quarter-final.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It means Humphries will have to wait to try and clinch his second Grand Slam title following his victory back in 2023.

"I was a bit nervous, but obviously I thought the game was over when I turned around and saw Luke hit the first treble 18 there, and hit the second one and then wired it," Sykes told Sky Sports following his win.

"I was so cold on that last one. I just thought, just hit it first out, no messing about, and get into it. And I did.

"I'm just riding a wave at the minute. I'm not really bothered who I play. I'll just come back up here and we'll see what happens."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

For Sykes, a mouth-watering clash with Michael van Gerwen awaits after he came through with a remarkable contest against James Wade with a 10-8 victory.

It marks Van Gerwen's first ranking quarter-final of 2026 and he earned it in some style with a near 104 average. There was nothing separating two darting juggernauts throughout the high-quality bout, a massive 121 checkout from the Dutchman levelling the game at 7-7 before rattling off two more legs to move 9-7 ahead.

Wade did not give up and a stunning 130 checkout, his second of the match, broke Van Gerwen's throw but the three-time Grand Slam champion broke straight back and pinned D16 for the win.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"To play in these types of games was even worse. I made it incredibly difficult for myself. That's sometimes so annoying," Van Gerwen told Sky Sports.

"I couldn't hit a double after the second break and with James Wade standing behind me - it's so annoying - but it's also his class. I dealt with it the right way, and now I feel comfortable now.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Sykes made it clear he would be making the match a real contest in the first session. He averaged 107.42 in a staggering opening five legs that saw him win four with incredible ease against the in-form player in the darting world.

Although still looking uncomfortable, Humphries fought back as Sykes went slightly off the boil. That saw him pick up four of the next five legs to level the game at 5-5.

The game continued to go back and forth as Humphries found some of his top levels, but Sykes would not back down, fighting back despite some strong finishing from 'Cool Hand', a 114 finish on tops the highlight.

It then looked like it was all going to go the way of Humphries when he powered in back-to-back 11-darters to take the game to a final-leg showdown but the 'Castleford Tiger' showed why he has become a formidable player.

Humphries missed D10 to finish off a 128 checkout which allowed Sykes to have his match dart at 36. He pinned that first dart for a win to remember.

Humphries took to social media after the contest to congratulate Sykes and admitted he has been through a tough 48 hours.

Humphries said: "Well done Tom Sykes absolutely amazing performance!

"So proud of the way I played tonight with what I've had to go through with injury the last 48 hours gave it my absolute all there.

"Wish everyone all the best for the rest of the tournament."

Sykes has been on the darting circuit since 2013 when he competed on the PDC Challenge Tour and then followed that up with a year on the PDC Development Tour.

It is over the last two years that Sykes has truly flourished. He qualified for the 2025 UK Open and made it all the way to the third round.

Earlier this year he clinched his Tour card at Q-School and has since made it to the fourth round at the UK Open before picking up the win of his career with the scalp of the world No 2 on the Grand Slam stage.

The 34-year-old hails from Castleford in West Yorkshire and his nickname 'The Castleford Tiger' is an ode to the rugby league side from his hometown.

Nathan Aspinall made it through to the quarter-finals with a hard-fought 10-7 victory over Gabriel Clemens.

Aspinall apologised post-match for "writing off" the German player before the game and it was clear why, with Clemens averaging 96.55 and hitting 10 180s.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

It was a topsy-turvy game throughout the first two sessions and at the end of them, the scores were level at 5-5.

However, it was from there that Aspinall took control. From 6-5 down, he took out four legs in a row and found a massive 'Big Fish' finish for a break of throw to send the Wolverhampton crowd wild.

Clemens did manage to get one more leg on the board but in the 17th leg, Aspinall scored highly and clinched D16 for a spot in the last eight.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

He will take on Gian van Veen after he held off a fightback from Martin Schindler for a 10-7 win.

It was in the second session that the world No 3 stepped things up. Averaging over 104, he took advantage of Schindler's clear issues on the doubles to take out four of the five legs to be 7-3 ahead.

Van Veen then made that seven out of eight legs and was one leg from victory before a period of poor scoring for the third seed and a massive improvement from Schindler saw the German take out four legs to put the pressure on.

Eventually, Van Veen found back-to-back 134s and took out 93 to book the showdown with Aspinall.

If there was any doubt over the scale of the task facing Mauricio Pochettino at Old Trafford, a social media exchange between one of his players and a content creator has illustrated it perfectly.

Manchester United winger Amad Diallo responded directly to an Instagram account criticising his recent display.

“Just shut your mouth, bro - you’re talking too much now,” Diallo wrote. “Go play in my place if it bothers you that much”.

While it is understandable for a young player to feel the weight of fan frustration, the optics of the situation are poor.

A Manchester United player reacting publicly to a troll on social media just days before a new manager takes charge is an indictment of the dressing room’s current mental state.

🚨📲 𝗡𝗘𝗪: Amad Diallo’s comment on a fan who criticized him: “Just shut your mouth, bro—you’re talking too much now. Go play in my place if it bothers you that much.” https://t.co/sLqd3B912HNovember 18, 2026

The incoming Pochettino will want an emotionally resilient squad, given the responsibility of representing one of the biggest clubs in world football.

This incident highlights the repair job required at Carrington, because if a highly-rated 24-year-old is spending his free time scrolling through his own mentions and biting back at criticism, it begs a much larger, more worrying question: Are all Manchester United players this hyper-aware of their online reception?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

If they are, it explains a great deal about the fragility on display during matches. A squad that lives and dies by its social media mentions is unequipped to handle the pressure cooker environment that is Old Trafford.

When things go wrong on the pitch - and they frequently do for this current iteration of Man United - players affected by outside noise are far more likely to retreat into their shells than rally together.

Pochettino’s first priority therefore cannot be tactical; it must be cultural. He has to insulate his squad from the news cycle which bounces between online praise and vitriol. The Argentine could do a lot worse than instituting a bunker mentality from day one at Old Trafford.

#1009. ‘He wants to change lives’: the story behind Bukayo Saka’s Sócrates award

By supporting the non-profit BigShoe, the Arsenal forward has earned deserved plaudits for his social conscience

Valerie Fiesser will never forget her surprise when Bukayo Saka contacted her out of the blue in 2022, asking whether he could help support a project in Nigeria. “I remember thinking: ‘Is this really Bukayo writing us an email?’” says the president of BigShoe, a non-profit organisation based in Frankfurt that has helped more than 10,000 children worldwide. “But that’s how he is. He’s always asking what more we can do.”

Four years on from that unexpected email, Fiesser was given the secret task of reaching out for a letter for Saka to read from the podium when he was presented with the Sócrates award at last month’s Ballon d’Or ceremony in London for his humanitarian work. She got the words from Byiringiro, a 14-year-old from Rwanda who had his eyesight restored after having surgery thanks to a BigShoe initiative.

“They told me he was going to receive the award, but he didn’t know, so they asked whether I could get a letter from one of the children we had helped,” Fiesser says. “I was really proud of Bukayo, I think the way he did it was really special. He stood there so strongly for all these children around the world that nobody sees and nobody hears. He gave them a voice. He took the attention away from himself and put it into action. That’s how I know Bukayo. It’s never about him, it’s always about the people we help. He’s incredible.”

Saka, who donated more than 1,000 school uniforms to children in his home borough of Ealing in west London last year to help with the cost of living crisis, is understood to have heard about BigShoe from Antonio Rüdiger after the Real Madrid and Germany defender told him about some of the work he had done with the organisation, including in Sierra Leone.

BigShoe has also worked with Philipp Lahm and Mesut Özil. Fiesser says Saka and his family have taken a particularly close interest in projects he supports.

“When we had 150 life-changing surgeries taking place in Nigeria, he would message me asking to see pictures,” she says. “He wanted to know what was happening and whether everybody was safe. He always asks whether the team has returned safely. I don’t know how he manages to find the time, but he does.

“His family are very similar. They genuinely want to make a big impact and provide meaningful help. I wouldn’t describe Bukayo as simply a donor to BigShoe. He’s more like a member of the BigShoe team. I know that he stands behind us.”

BigShoe was established by four friends in Germany after the 2006 World Cup. As part of its latest projects in Rwanda and Nigeria, about 3,000 people had eye examinations and were given glasses if required. “Giving a child a pair of glasses can change their life,” Fiesser says. “We also help entire families. If a father can’t see properly, he might not be able to work or read. That affects the whole family.”

BigShoe recently renovated a school in Rwanda and provided clean drinking water through a filtration system. It has also built a library and provided private changing facilities for girls. “Once a month, some girls miss school because they don’t have suitable facilities or somewhere private to change,” says Fiesser. “We built facilities so they can continue attending school and have a quiet, private area.”

A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis

Saka’s hectic playing schedule means he has yet to make a visit, but his family have been on the ground in Rwanda and he was heavily involved in funding earthquake relief projects in Morocco and Turkey. “We provided container homes for people affected by the earthquakes,” says Fiesser. “I knew I could count on him. It’s always important to Bukayo that we make a big impact. He doesn’t want money to be wasted. When I present a project to him, he wants to understand it properly. He needs to know exactly what we’re doing before he makes a decision. He’s a 100% person. Whatever he does, he gives it everything.”

Saka’s mother, Adenike, is believed to be a driving force behind her son’s charitable work. Fiesser describes her as “one of the most amazing women I’ve met”. Plans are being made for the next projects, which include providing health insurance to families in Nigeria and food packages for children in Rwanda over Christmas, even if Saka has typically been pushing for something more long-term.

“He doesn’t just want to give someone food,” Fiesser says. “Of course, food is important, and we’re providing that too, but he wants to change lives. You can help someone, but if the help doesn’t last, then it hasn’t achieved what you really wanted. If we all work together, it doesn’t matter which team we’re supporting or which country we’re helping. We’re all part of one world.”

#1008. Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?

France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) buildout, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued about $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.

Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.

Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.

That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.

The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.

Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."

That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.

Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.

The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.

The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.

The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino was only hired after conversations with a leftfield former Chelsea player.

That's according to a new report, which says that Manchester United had an exhaustive list of options to manage the club, including surprise names, with different figures pulling in different directions behind the scenes.

Pochettino is taking over while the Red Devils are in the relegation zone, with the likes of Cesc Fabregas having been touted for the job – but it was another former Chelsea star who perhaps came closer to getting the nod.

#1006. Sykes ready to go 'all the way' on debut at Grand Slam after stunning Humphries

Tom Sykes came up with a thrilling 10-9 victory over Luke Humphries at the Grand Slam of Darts; It sees him through to the quarter-finals on debut; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Sports Journalist @MegWellensX

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Tom Sykes pulled off the biggest win of his darting career with a 10-9 victory over Luke Humphries in the last 16 at the Grand Slam of Darts - but he does not want to stop there.

The 'Castleford Tiger', who is making his debut in Wolverhampton, put in an incredible performance against the world No 2 in which he raced away before 'Cool Hand' fought back to take the game to a last-leg decider.

Sykes scored amazingly in that winner-takes-all leg and with Humphries unable to finish off the 128 checkout, he clinched D18 to set up a quarter-final showdown with Michael van Gerwen after his 10-8 win over James Wade in the final match of the night.

Sykes is ranked 72nd in the world in what is his first year on the PDC Pro Tour but, with the way he is playing, he sees no reason why he cannot go on a real run at the Grand Slam.

"I think so. I know I have got the scoring game," Sykes said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

"I know I have got the scoring game to live with anyone in the world, and I have shown it tonight with the 180s and the 140s that I have been hitting.

"If the doubles go in, then I'm a dangerous player."

Humphries was suffering with a shoulder injury throughout the contest and Sykes did not realise until they were practicing and was gingerly picking up his darts.

Despite the clear pain Humphries was in, Sykes still feels he was up against the best darts player in the world playing some of the best darts in the world.

"I can't believe it, honestly. Luke didn't tell me till the end, but he said he had a bit of an injury there. I could tell, to be fair," he added.

"In the practice darts at the beginning, he was dropping his darts and he could barely bend over to pick them up.

"He still played really well and I got off to a really good start. To get 4-1 up against, in my opinion, the best player in the world at the minute, I'm absolutely buzzing with that.

"For me, he is still one of the best players in the world, even if he's injured or not. I am just buzzing to get the win over him."

Many a player would be overawed with the experiences that Sykes is now having but, as someone who enjoys the big stages, he is revelling in rubbing shoulders with the top stars of the sport.

"When I first started on the Pro Tour and I'm walking in, you see Luke Humphries, Luke Littler, Michael van Gerwen, James Wade. It is a bit daunting walking in and seeing all these guys who you've watched on TV," Sykes said.

"I massively put the hard work in for the last year, and I ended up getting my Tour card last year, and now I'm reaping the rewards of it."

#1005. European football body’s plan to go global leaves Fifa on tenterhooks

Findings of ‘feasibility study’ into quest for world domination loom with Europe’s wealthiest certain to benefit whatever the outcome

It will be one of the most eagerly devoured documents in football circles, assuming its contents are ever fully revealed. In September, the increasingly powerful European Football Clubs body announced a “feasibility study” into how it can become established on a more global scale, morphing into an organisation that represents clubs all over the world.

The study’s findings could, some leading figures in the sport’s governance believe, define football’s long-term future. It has the potential to transform a landscape destabilised by the scandals surrounding Fifa and Gianni Infantino.

Once considered a lobby group representing clubs’ interests in the face of domineering governing bodies, EFC has mushroomed into a behemoth with almost 1,000 members that has the potential to supplant those bodies.

“Now is the time to create World Football Clubs,” the EFC chair, Nasser Al-Khelaïfi, told delegates at its general assembly in Copenhagen seven weeks ago. The desire to expand exists in plain sight and is perfectly natural, some with a close interest in the process point out, given players and domestic leagues already have their own global representative bodies.

However, others warn of “a takeover by stealth” and fear it is merely a fig leaf for the tightening of the top European clubs’ influence over the game’s shape.

Sources familiar with EFC’s intentions say it is examining how to enter the international football market as a competition organiser, floating the idea of organising more effective tournaments in different formats. That is the role of Fifa or continental organisations such as Uefa and Concacaf but, should leading clubs find a way to forge events of their own, they could reap financial and commercial benefits far beyond those on offer through the confederations.

The prospect has some of the established powers on high alert. “You’re starting to see one of the major unspoken faultlines in football open up,” one source says of EFC’s relationship with Uefa, which has become structurally closer in recent years, but is still conducted with an air of high mutual caution. “Friends close, enemies closer” is one characterisation of that relationship.

This particularly appears the case now that, in the wreckage of Infantino’s doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, all parties find themselves jostling for leverage. Beyond a dramatic increase in funding for the member associations, many senior figures in football have remarked that the biggest long-term consequence of FFE’s failure will be to increase the power of the biggest European clubs.

While the former development is already in motion, with Fifa announcing last month that it will hand over an additional $2.7bn (£2.05bn) from its reserves over the next four years, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn, the latter will not be far behind.

That is because EFC’s study is not alone in harbouring huge implications for football’s shape. As revealed in September, a joint venture between EFC and Fifa to run the commercial side of global club competitions like the Club World Cup has been in the works for some time, with the fallout from FFE emerging as the catalyst required to push it through.

Multiple sources say the joint venture, similar to the agreement under which Uefa and EFC have operated European club competitions since 2008 that was formalised last year with the creation of commercial entity UC3, is ready to proceed pending approval from Infantino.

One source with knowledge of the discussions claims Infantino had been holding up the deal until the FFE scandal broke in July, since when negotiations have accelerated. An announcement could be made at next month’s Fifa council meeting in Doha, although waiting until after March’s presidential election at the global governing body seems more likely.

The joint venture’s contents have caused particular concern within Uefa, whose hierarchy are believed to have made clear their wish that a deal between EFC and Fifa is not rushed through.

While Uefa have continued to attack Infantino forcibly and are on the verge of backing a candidate to stand against him in next year’s election, EFC has been largely silent since its chief executive, Charlie Marshall, sent an explosive letter to Fifa’s secretary general, Mattias Grafström, on 31 July.

EFC strongly condemned FFE, with the Guardian revealing the body threatened to boycott future Club World Cups (CWC) and withdraw its endorsement of the international match calendar. The sell-off plan was formally dropped the following day.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

One particularly incendiary section read: “Unless a fully operational Fifa-EFC CWC joint venture, with exclusive authority over, among other things, all commercial and operational matters, is established well ahead of the women’s 2028 Fifa CWC rights cycle, EFC will not support – and its member clubs will not participate in – any future edition, including the women’s and men’s 2028 and 2029 Fifa CWC.”

Al-Khelaïfi, who is also the president of Paris Saint-Germain, did not directly address the issue during his speech in Copenhagen two months later and there are suggestions a mutually beneficial solution has been reached. The crisis may have landed EFC the terms they wanted.

“It’s not a matter of whether Gianni wins [the election], but what his mandate is, and who is behind it,” a senior source in European football said. “A large part of the answer is EFC. EFC is going to take over Fifa in the same way [it] took over Uefa. The big clubs have gained yet more power and control.

“EFC initially came out very hard against Gianni, but were quick to row back. They’ve been silent on the presidential election and other governance issues, as it’s clear they’ve reached an agreement with Fifa. The joint venture is the price of their silence.”

The result is likely to be an acceleration of trends already under way. The biggest European clubs look set to make even more money from new tournaments, particularly given they are likely to increase in size and regularity, beginning with a 48-team men’s Club World Cup in 2029.

Chelsea earned $115m (£85m) from winning the inaugural expanded tournament last year, with six European clubs in the top seven of the prize money table and Brazil’s Fluminense the only non-European side to earn more than $50m. Solidarity payments are also skewed towards Europe, whose clubs will receive 50% of the $250m pot despite providing only 12 of the 32 contestants. Those defending the status quo note that Europe generates about 70% of Fifa’s revenue.

A senior source at another confederation said the inevitable result of the joint venture would be less money for the rest of the world, certainly in proportional terms. “The most significant long-term result of the Fifa crisis will be to entrench the economic might of the biggest European clubs,” they said. “That means reduced access to competitions, less revenue and broadcast rights for the rest of us.

“The European clubs are well organised, economically rational and have taken advantage of the opportunity to extract something from Fifa. Gianni Infantino is in the business of writing cheques and will now be writing big ones to clubs as well as member associations.”

These developments are, at least, easily foreseeable. It is less straightforward to analyse how football’s face will change if a putative World Football Clubs gains the power many believe lies in its sights. “Every club around the world deserves to be represented; to have a voice, and a better chance to succeed,” Al-Khelaïfi said in his September address. But the world’s wealthiest clubs stand poised to benefit from football’s crisis more handsomely than anyone.

#1004. Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict

The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several Houthi attacks of late.

A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.

The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.

Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.

Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."

It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

"The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.

"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.

However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

New Manchester United manager Mauricio Pochettino is starting his to-do list with a shock departure

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Manchester United could be about to make a shock sale, which would divide the fans.

The business would represent the first major transfer market activity of new manager Mauricio Pochettino, who arrived at Manchester United this week after two years in charge of the United States men's national team.

With the Red Devils languishing in the relegation zone, it's accepted that the club will have to recruit to turn fortunes around – but there may well be a clearout, too, of underperformers.

With many of the squad that Pochettino has inherited coming under fire this season, there could be major exits in the upcoming January transfer window.

32-year-old club captain Bruno Fernandes' future is uncertain, World Cup winner Lisandro Martinez has hit out at directors behind the scenes and Marcus Rashford has been linked with a permanent departure after Michael Carrick reintegrated him at Carrington – but now another name has emerged as a move that should split the fanbase.

Sport Witness have relayed a report from Turkish outlet Sabah on Amad Diallo's future, with Besiktas keen on signing the wide man.

Both Vaclav Cerny and Ernest Poku have struggled for the Black Eagles, who are apparently looking to the Premier League for a new option on the right flank.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

The report mentions that Aston Villa were interested in the Ivorian over the summer, but with Bryan Mbeumo the first choice on the right wing – and only filling in up front in the absence of Benjamin Sesko – Amad's role is a little unclear in the squad.

Having made just four senior appearances at Atalanta, Amad joined United in 2021 in a late-window move before heading on loan to Rangers and Sunderland to develop further.

He returned for the 2023/24 season – getting sent off against Liverpool in March 2024 for a second yellow card when he removed his shirt in celebration of scoring the winner – but after establishing himself as a linchpin of Ruben Amorim's back three system, the 24-year-old has just two assists since the Portuguese was relieved of duties in the dugout, with his last goal coming almost a year ago.

Despite this, United fans would likely be torn on his exit: while Amad isn't in good form and hasn't shown that he can become a world-beater by any stretch, he is certainly not one of the club's bigger problems and turfing out a solid squad player when there are such glaring issues across the pitch perhaps isn't a priority.

It remains to be seen whether Pochettino will revert to his Tottenham Hotspur days and occasionally employ wing-backs, or whether he will only use a back four at Old Trafford.

Amad is worth €45 million, as per Transfermarkt. United face Liverpool when Premier League action resumes this weekend.
